procedural_history.originating_court: Special Court, ASJ/05, PMLA, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 22.09.2023 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi, in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 2408/2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant initially filed a bail application before the Special Court on 12.07.2023, which was dismissed on 22.07.2023. The appellant then filed a Writ Petition (Crl.) No.336/2023 before the Supreme Court challenging the order dated 22.07.2023 passed by the Special Court dismissing his bail application. This was withdrawn with liberty to approach the High Court. Subsequently, the appellant filed Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 2408/2023 in the High Court of Delhi, seeking a declaration that his arrest on 27.06.2023 was illegal and violative of fundamental rights, a direction to release him, and to quash the remand order dated 28.06.2023. The High Court dismissed this petition on 22.09.2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's judgment and order dated 22.09.2023. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal, finding it devoid of merit.

issue.issue_text: Whether the action of the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in handing over the document containing the grounds of arrest to an arrestee, having them read and sign it, and then taking the document back without providing a copy at the time of arrest, renders the arrest illegal under Section 19 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

facts: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) arrested the appellant under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
At the time of arrest, the ED handed the appellant a document containing the written grounds for his arrest.
The appellant read the grounds, made an endorsement on the document stating he had been informed, and signed it.
The ED then took the document back without providing a copy to the appellant at that specific moment.
The appellant did not dispute that he was shown the grounds or that he signed the document.
law: Section 19 of the PMLA and Article 22(1) of the Constitution of India mandate that an arrested person must be informed of the grounds for their arrest.
The Supreme Court interpreted this requirement to mean that the person must be made aware of the grounds of arrest at the time of the arrest.
The Court distinguished between the act of "informing" the person at the time of arrest and the act of "furnishing" a written copy.
The Court noted that furnishing a written copy "as soon as may be" or within 24 hours of the arrest would be sufficient compliance with the law.
application: The Court applied the law to the undisputed facts of the case.

It determined that by handing the document to the appellant, allowing him to read it, and obtaining his signed endorsement confirming he was informed, the ED had fulfilled its legal obligation to "inform" him of the grounds of arrest.
The Court found that this action constituted due compliance with the provisions of Section 19 of the PMLA and Article 22(1) of the Constitution.

The appellant's sole contention—that he was not given a copy to keep at the moment of arrest—was deemed insufficient to invalidate the arrest, as the primary requirement of being informed had been met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge and held that the arrest was not illegal. The Court concluded that since the appellant was indisputably informed of the grounds of arrest by being allowed to read and sign the document, the requirements of Section 19 of the PMLA were satisfied, even though a physical copy was not left with him at the exact time of arrest.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the action of the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in handing over the document containing the grounds of arrest to an arrestee, having them read and sign it, and then taking the document back without providing a copy at the time of arrest, renders the arrest illegal under Section 19 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, relying on the precedent set in 'Pankaj Bansal vs. Union of India', argued that the arrest was illegal.

They contended that merely informing the accused orally, allowing them to read the grounds of arrest, and obtaining a signature on the document without providing a written copy to the arrestee is not in consonance with the law.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (ED) argued that the appellant was, in fact, handed the document containing the grounds of arrest at the time of his arrest.

They pointed out that the appellant acknowledged this by making an endorsement stating, 'I have been informed and have also read the above-mentioned grounds of arrest,' and then signed the document, which the appellant did not dispute.
This procedure, they contended, fulfills the requirement of contemporaneously informing the arrested person about the grounds of their arrest.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statement of law by a Division Bench is binding on a Division Bench of the same or a lesser number of judges. If a bench concludes that an earlier judgment of a larger bench is incorrect, the proper course is to refer the matter to a bench of the same size as the one that delivered the earlier judgment, outlining the reasons for the disagreement.
obiter: The doctrine of binding precedent promotes certainty, consistency, and the organic development of law.
It is of paramount importance for the law declared by the Supreme Court to be certain, clear, and consistent due to the hierarchical nature of the judicial system.
Most court decisions are significant not merely for adjudicating the rights of the parties but also because they embody a declaration of law that operates as a binding principle in future cases.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the procedure followed by the Enforcement Directorate—handing the written grounds of arrest to the appellant, allowing him to read them, and obtaining his signed endorsement acknowledging that he had been informed of and had read the grounds—satisfied the legal requirement under Section 19 of the PMLA to "inform" an arrestee of the grounds for their arrest. The subsequent act of taking the document back without providing a copy at that specific moment did not render the arrest illegal, as the statutory mandate to inform the person had been fulfilled contemporaneously with the arrest.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of the statutory mandate under Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, specifically what constitutes 'informing' an arrested person of the grounds of arrest.

Application of the doctrine of binding precedent, particularly the prospective effect of the ruling in 'Pankaj Bansal vs. Union of India' which mandated that, 'henceforth,' a copy of the written grounds of arrest must be furnished to the arrested person.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's central argument that merely allowing a perusal of the grounds of arrest without providing a copy is illegal was rejected because the court found the respondent's actions sufficient to meet the statutory requirement of 'informing' the arrestee.

The appellant's own signed endorsement on the grounds of arrest, stating, 'I have been informed and have also read the above-mentioned grounds of arrest,' directly contradicted his claim and served as evidence that he was, in fact, properly informed at the time of arrest.

The appellant's assertion that the failure to provide a copy was an incurable illegality was not accepted, as the court determined that the core legal requirement to inform the arrestee of the grounds had been met through the process of showing, reading, and signing the document.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that their procedure fulfilled the requirement of contemporaneously informing the arrested person about the grounds of their arrest.

The respondent provided crucial evidence in the form of the grounds of arrest document which contained the appellant's own signed acknowledgment that he had been informed of and had read the grounds, a fact the appellant did not dispute.

The court accepted the respondent's contention that handing over the document for reading and obtaining a signed acknowledgment constitutes a valid fulfillment of the duty to 'inform' the arrestee under Section 19 of the PMLA.
policy_considerations: The doctrine of binding precedent has the merit of promoting a certainty and consistency in judicial decisions, and enables an organic development of the law, besides providing assurance to the individual as to the consequence of transactions forming part of his daily aﬀairs.
Taking note of the hierarchical character of the judicial system in India, it is of paramount importance that the law declared by this Court should be certain, clear and consistent.

The discipline demanded by a precedent or the disqualification or diminution of a decision on the application of the per incuriam rule is of great importance, since without it, certainty of law, consistency of rulings and comity of courts would become a costly casualty.
